svg.aria-label: Diagram: the Shared VPC IAM model, where the Shared VPC Admin is a pair of roles and the second one is what grants the power to share all existing and future subnets; the network admin split in which Network Admin controls every network resource except firewall rules and SSL certificates which belong to Security Admin, and Network User is a different role again; the lien that protects a host project from deletion and which a project owner can remove by default unless an organization constraint restricts it; the billing link whose disconnection shuts down every dependent service project; and the machine principals, where each service project needs two service agents granted in the host project and the console grants one of them silently while the CLI does not
svg.title: Shared VPC IAM: a two-role admin, a three-way network split, a removable lien, and two robot accounts per service project
svg.text: Shared VPC needs a minimum of three admin roles, and the humans are not the only principals.
The protection against deleting the host project is, by default, removable by its own owner.
The admin is a PAIR of roles, and the second one is the powerful half
compute.xpnAdmin enables host projects and attaches service projects. Without it you cannot
even SEE the Shared VPC page in the console.
Project IAM Admin is what grants permission to share ALL EXISTING AND FUTURE SUBNETS,
not just individual ones. The broad-share power lives in the IAM role, not the XPN one.
Bound at ORGANIZATION OR FOLDER level, never project — so the principal must exist in the org.
Three roles with similar names that do different things
NETWORK ADMIN: full control of all network resources EXCEPT firewall rules and SSL certs.
SECURITY ADMIN: exactly those two — firewall rules and SSL certificates.
NETWORK USER: not an admin at all. It is the grant that lets a service project CONSUME a
subnet. The docs flag it: the Network User and Network Admin roles are DIFFERENT.
So routing, filtering and consuming are three separable jobs. Most estates grant them as one.
The lien, and why it is weaker than it sounds
Deleting a host project would cause OUTAGES IN ALL ATTACHED SERVICE PROJECTS. So enabling
one places a lien on it, and the lien is removed automatically when Shared VPC is turned off.
BY DEFAULT A PROJECT OWNER CAN REMOVE THE LIEN, then delete the project. The docs say so
outright. Removal needs projects.get and projects.updateLiens.
The fix is one organization constraint — compute.restrictXpnProjectLienRemoval — which
confines removal to org-level owners or lienModifier. Set once, covers every project.
The other way to take everything down
Disconnecting BILLING on a Shared VPC network can lead to a COMPLETE SHUTDOWN of all
dependent resources, INCLUDING SERVICE PROJECTS.
No lien guards that path. The billing link is a separate thing to secure, and a billing
administrator is usually not the person the network runbook names.
The principals nobody puts in the runbook: two robots per service project
For GKE, each service project needs its GKE service agent granted HOST SERVICE AGENT USER on
the host, acting there AS IF IT WERE the host’s own agent. Grantable to nothing else.
AND Compute Network User must be added MANUALLY to that agent — enabling GKE access does
not do it. Two agents need it: container-engine-robot and cloudservices.
CONSOLE grants Host Service Agent User for you on attach. gcloud does not. #73’s divergence,
a third time.
Both post-attach defaults are permissive: any non-host may attach to any host in the org, and
principals may use any subnet they hold permissions on. Two constraints narrow each.
